claims.claim: MChIP-C achieves superior sensitivity and resolution compared to C-methods based on standard restriction enzymes.
claims.source: Thus, in line with other recent reports on MNase-based C-methods (Hsieh et al., 2020; Krietenstein et al., 2020; Hua et al., 2021; Aljahani et al., 2022; Goel et al., 2022; Ramasamy et al., 2022), our results suggest that MChIP-C achieves superior sensitivity and resolution compared to C-methods based on standard restriction enzymes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analyses with PLAC-seq and Hi-C, and is consistent with published reports on MNase-based methods.

claims.claim: In the context of promoter-centered interactions, MChIP-C outperforms standard whole-genome Micro-C.
claims.source: Additionally, in the context of promoter-centered interactions, our results suggest that MChIP-C also outperforms standard whole-genome Micro-C.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analyses with Micro-C shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claims.claim: About half of the identified promoter-CTCF interactions (19,773 out of 38,271) showed CTCF binding at the promoter side as well.
claims.source: About half of the identified promoter-CTCF interactions (19,773 out of 38,271) showed CTCF binding at the promoter side as well.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CTCF binding at both ends of promoter-CTCF interactions.

claims.claim: Only 540 (~2.7%) of promoter-CTCF interactions with CTCF binding on both sides directly correspond to CTCF-CTCF loops reported in a previous Hi-C study.
claims.source: Interestingly, only 540 (~2.7%) of those directly correspond to CTCF-CTCF loops reported in a previous Hi-C study (Rao et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published Hi-C loop data from Rao et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Promoters preferentially interact with CTCF-bound sites if CTCF motifs are oriented towards the promoter (79% towards vs 21% away).
claims.source: We found that promoters preferentially interact with CTCF-bound sites if CTCF motifs are oriented towards the promoter (79% towards vs 21% away) (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CTCF motif orientation in PIRs shown in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: The CTCF orientation bias holds true regardless of the position of the CTCF site relative to the transcription direction (80% vs 20% for upstream CTCF sites and 79% vs 21% for downstream sites).
claims.source: This bias holds true regardless of the position of the CTCF site relative to the transcription direction (80% vs 20% for upstream CTCF sites and 79% vs 21% for downstream sites).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CTCF motif orientation stratified by position relative to the promoter.

claims.claim: The CTCF orientation bias is observed regardless of CTCF binding at the promoter side.
claims.source: We conclude that interactions of promoters with CTCF-bound sites are biased by CTCF orientation, regardless of CTCF binding at the promoter side.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The CTCF orientation bias suggests the possible involvement of loop extrusion.
claims.source: This orientation bias suggests the possible involvement of loop extrusion.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed CTCF orientation bias and knowledge of loop extrusion mechanisms.

claims.claim: Most of the analyzed transcription-related factors and histone post-translational modifications are substantially enriched in MChIP-C PIRs (4–25 X).
claims.source: Most of the analyzed transcription-related factors and histone post-translational modifications are substantially enriched in MChIP-C PIRs (4–25 X; Figure 3b; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis of 271 ChIP-seq profiles in PIRs shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: H3K27me3 is not enriched in MChIP-C PIRs (1137 overlaps, 1953 [SD = 44] expected by chance).
claims.source: Notable exceptions are facultative heterochromatin-associated histone mark H3K27me3 (1137 overlaps, 1953 [SD = 44] expected by chance) and LINE1-binding protein ZNF146 (183 overlaps, 180 [SD = 12] expected by chance).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis comparing observed vs expected overlaps.

claims.claim: CTCF, RAD21, and SMC3 are among the most highly enriched factors in MChIP-C PIRs.
claims.source: As expected, CTCF (22,943/1679 [SD = 41]), cohesin subunits RAD21 (10,702/413 [SD = 23]) and SMC3 (12,956/576 [SD = 27]) are among the most highly enriched factors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Hierarchical clustering of PIR-overlapping DHSs identified four major clusters based on transcription factor binding profiles.
claims.source: Rather than separately consider each factor associated with a PIR, we next used hierarchical clustering to partition PIR-overlapping DHSs (i.e. promoter interacting DHSs; N=19,129) into groups according to the factor binding profile of each DHS. We identified four major clusters (Figure 3c; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: Clusters 1 and 2 DHSs were almost universally bound by CTCF (98.1% and 93.6%), cohesin subunits SMC3 (87.5% and 66.9%) and RAD21 (73.6% and 52.9%), and ZNF143 (87.3% and 66.3%).
claims.source: Clusters 1 (N=4447) and 2 (N=4791) were almost universally bound by the structural factors CTCF (98.1% and 93.6% in clusters 1 and 2 correspondingly), cohesin subunits SMC3 (87.5% and 66.9%) and RAD21 (73.6% and 52.9%) as well as zinc finger protein ZNF143 (87.3% and 66.3%).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TRF binding in clustered DHSs shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: 24,331 interactions with a median distance of ~92 kb were anchored in DHSs from clusters 1 and 2.
claims.source: A total of 24,331 interactions with a median distance of ~92 kb were anchored in DHSs from these two clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of interaction distances for different DHS clusters shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claims.claim: DHSs from clusters 3 and 4 contained almost no CTCF- or cohesin-bound sites but were enriched in dozens of transcription-related factors.
claims.source: DHSs from clusters 3 (N = 3168) and 4 (N=6723) contained almost no CTCF- or cohesin-bound sites but they were enriched in dozens of transcription-related factors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TRF binding in clustered DHSs shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: CRISPRi-confirmed enhancers were significantly overrepresented in cluster 3 DHSs (171/297 overlaps; one-sided binomial test, p=1.64*10–57).
claims.source: Notably, CRISPRi-confirmed enhancers (Fulco et al., 2019; Gasperini et al., 2019) were significantly overrepresented in cluster 3 DHSs (171/297 overlaps; one-sided binomial test, p=1.64*10–57), and we thus labeled P-cluster 3 DHS interactions as regulatory interactions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of enhancer enrichment in cluster 3 DHSs.

claims.claim: There were 7214 regulatory interactions, which tended to be shorter (median length ~47 kb) than structural interactions.
claims.source: Overall, there were 7214 regulatory interactions, which tended to be shorter (median length ~47 kb) than structural ones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of interaction distances shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claims.claim: Cohesin subunits were absent in the vast majority of class 3 DHSs, indicating that cohesin may not be involved in the maintenance of regulatory interactions.
claims.source: Interestingly, cohesin subunits were absent in the vast majority of class 3 DHSs. In agreement with a number of recent observations (Thiecke et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2022) this may indicate that cohesin is not involved in the maintenance of the regulatory interactions, albeit such a role was suggested earlier (Kagey et al., 2010; Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the observed absence of cohesin in cluster 3 DHSs and is supported by citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: An initial random forest model consisting of genomic distance, CTCF ChIP-seq signal, and motif orientations was able to explain ~37% of variance in the MChIP-C signal.
claims.source: The initial random forest model consisted of five features: DHS-promoter genomic distance, CTCF ChIP-seq signal at both the promoter and the DHS, and motif orientations on both the promoter and the DHS. This initial model was able to explain ~37% of variance in the MChIP-C signal.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by random forest modeling results shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: Adding RAD21 and EP300 to the random forest model increased predictive performance to an R2 of ~43%.
claims.source: Then, we iteratively added the most predictive feature out of a set of 270 ChIP-seq profiles, where predictivity is calculated as R2 in threefold cross-validation. Using this strategy, cohesin subunit RAD21 and histone acetyltransferase EP300 were automatically selected, after which predictive performance plateaued at an R2 of ~43% (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by greedy forward feature selection results shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: EP300 was threefold enriched in cluster 3 DHSs and 92.2% of cluster 3 DHSs showed EP300 binding.
claims.source: As CTCF and RAD21 are mostly associated with structural loops, we asked whether EP300 mainly underlies regulatory interactions. Indeed, we find that EP300 was threefold enriched in cluster 3 DHSs and 92.2% of cluster 3 DHSs showed EP300 binding.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of EP300 binding in cluster 3 DHSs.

claims.claim: The only proteins that had more binding sites in cluster 3 DHSs than EP300 are subunits of the SWI/SNF remodeling complex: DPF2 (97.8%), ARID1B (95.6%), and SMARCE1 (94.3%).
claims.source: Interestingly, we noticed that the only proteins that had more binding sites in cluster 3 DHSs are subunits of the SWI/SNF remodeling complex: DPF2 (97.8%), ARID1B (95.6%), and SMARCE1 (94.3%; Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TRF binding in cluster 3 DHSs shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: EP300 has been found to directly interact with SWI/SNF-complex.
claims.source: EP300 has been found to directly interact with SWI/SNF-complex (Alver et al., 2017; Blümli et al., 2021) and their chromatin binding profiles are highly correlated (Pearson correlation 0.65–0.70).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating EP300-SWI/SNF interaction and by correlation analysis of their binding profiles.

claims.claim: The chromatin binding profiles of EP300 and SWI/SNF subunits are highly correlated (Pearson correlation 0.65–0.70).
claims.source: EP300 has been found to directly interact with SWI/SNF-complex (Alver et al., 2017; Blümli et al., 2021) and their chromatin binding profiles are highly correlated (Pearson correlation 0.65–0.70).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of ChIP-seq profiles.

claims.claim: The predictive power of SWI/SNF subunits is very close to that of EP300.
claims.source: Revisiting the binding profiles of these SWI/SNF subunits, we found their predictive power to be very close to that of EP300 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by random forest modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claims.claim: RNA polymerase II, mediator complex, YY1 and BRD4 are weaker predictors of MChIP-C signal than EP300 and the SWI/SNF subunits.
claims.source: We also specifically examined the predictive power of RNA polymerase II, mediator complex, YY1 and BRD4, which were previously suggested to be associated with enhancer-promoter interaction (Papantonis and Cook, 2011; Kagey et al., 2010; Weintraub et al., 2017; Hnisz et al., 2017), and find that while they individually have some predictive power, they are weaker predictors of MChIP-C signal than EP300 and the SWI/SNF subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by random forest modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: EP300 and/or the SWI/SNF complex might be involved in the formation of regulatory chromatin interactions independently of СTCF and cohesin.
claims.source: Thus, we suggest that EP300 and/or the SWI/SNF complex might be involved in the formation of regulatory chromatin interactions independently of СTCF and cohesin.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the predictive power of EP300 and SWI/SNF in the absence of CTCF/cohesin in regulatory interactions.

claims.claim: 60.7% (222/366, 95% CI [55.7%; 65.7%]) of functionally verified E-P pairs have underlying spatial interactions detected with MChIP-C.
claims.source: Notably, we found that 60.7% (222/366, 95% CI [55.7%; 65.7%]) of the verified pairs have underlying spatial interactions detected with MChIP-C, while only 6.5% (3,554/54,811, 95% CI [6.3%; 6.7%]) of non-regulatory DHS-P pairs show such interactions (Figure 4a and b; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of MChIP-C interactions with CRISPRi-validated E-P pairs shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: Only 6.5% (3,554/54,811, 95% CI [6.3%; 6.7%]) of non-regulatory DHS-P pairs show spatial interactions in MChIP-C.
claims.source: Notably, we found that 60.7% (222/366, 95% CI [55.7%; 65.7%]) of the verified pairs have underlying spatial interactions detected with MChIP-C, while only 6.5% (3,554/54,811, 95% CI [6.3%; 6.7%]) of non-regulatory DHS-P pairs show such interactions (Figure 4a and b; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of MChIP-C interactions with non-functional DHS-P pairs shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: A majority of experimentally validated enhancers exhibit interaction with their target promoters.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that a majority of experimentally validated enhancers exhibit interaction with their target promoters.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the finding that 60.7% of CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs show MChIP-C interactions.

claims.claim: The recall of MChIP-C (60.7%) was superior to those of PLAC-seq (14.0%), Micro-C (19.9%), and Hi-C (2.2%) for detecting CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs.
claims.source: With respect to recall/sensitivity, the recall of MChIP-C (60.7%, as mentioned above) was superior to those of PLAC-seq (14.0%), Micro-C (19.9%), and Hi-C (2.2%).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by systematic comparison of different C-methods' ability to detect CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The precision of MChIP-C (5.9%) was comparable to PLAC-seq (4.0%), Micro-C (7.4%), and Hi-C (2.4%).
claims.source: In spite of this, the precision of the methods was comparable, with 5.9% for MChIP-C, 4.0% for PLAC-seq, 7.4% for Micro-C, and 2.4% for Hi-C.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by systematic comparison of different C-methods shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 50% down-sampled MChIP-C maintains a high recall of 56.1%, with slightly better precision (6.3%) and false positive rate (5.5%).
claims.source: Evaluating predictive performance after down-sampling, we find that 50% down-sampled MChIP-C maintains a high recall of 56.1%, with slightly better precision (6.3%) and false positive rate (5.5%).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of down-sampled MChIP-C data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: At 10% down-sampling, MChIP-C achieves a better precision (10.4%) and false positive rate (1%) than competing methods, while its recall (18.2%) is slightly worse than Micro-C but better than PLAC-Seq and Hi-C.
claims.source: Even at 10% down-sampling, MChIP-C achieves a better precision (10.4%) and false positive rate (1%) than the competing methods, while its recall (18.2%) is slightly worse than that of Micro-C but better than those of PLAC-Seq and Hi-C.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of down-sampled MChIP-C data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The enhanced sensitivity of MChIP-C enables detection of a larger and more precise set of enhancer-promoter interactions than the alternatives.
claims.source: In summary, these results suggest that the enhanced sensitivity of MChIP-C enables detection of a larger and more precise set of enhancer-promoter interactions than the alternatives.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the comparative analysis of MChIP-C with other C-methods.

claims.claim: In some instances, weak interactions were visually apparent but were missed by the interaction calling algorithm, especially in viewpoints that had low coverage.
claims.source: First, we noticed that, in some instances, weak interactions were visually apparent but were missed by the interaction calling algorithm, especially in viewpoints that had low coverage (Figure 4b, iv).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of MChIP-C profiles for validated E-P pairs without called interactions.

claims.claim: When considering 185/366 validated E-P pairs corresponding to high-coverage viewpoints, 68.1% (126/185, 95% CI [61.4%; 74.8%]) had underlying MChIP-C spatial interactions.
claims.source: Indeed, when we considered 185/366 validated E-P pairs corresponding to high-coverage viewpoints, 68.1% (126/185, 95% CI [61.4%; 74.8%]) had underlying MChIP-C spatial interactions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reanalysis of high-coverage viewpoints.

claims.claim: In some cases, adjacent H3K27ac-positive regions clearly interacting with the expected promoter were observed, possibly suggesting inexact identification of the enhancer position due to the limited resolution of the CRISPRi screens.
claims.source: Second, in some cases we noticed adjacent (few kb) H3K27ac-positive regions clearly interacting with the expected promoter, possibly suggesting inexact identification of the enhancer position due to the limited resolution of the CRISPRi screens (Gasperini et al., 2019; Figure 4b, v).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of MChIP-C profiles and is supported by a citation discussing CRISPRi screen resolution.

claims.claim: CRISPRi-detected E-P interactions are not guaranteed to represent direct effects, as an enhancer may impose secondary influence through the action of the directly targeted gene.
claims.source: Third, CRISPRi-detected E-P interactions are not guaranteed to represent direct effects. In some cases, an enhancer may impose secondary influence through the action of the directly targeted gene (Gasperini et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the CRISPRi study and by a specific example (LMO2-CAT).

claims.claim: The genomic distance between non-interacting E-P pairs (median 71 kb) is substantially larger than between interacting E-P pairs (median 30 kb).
claims.source: Indeed, we observed that the genomic distance between non-interacting E-P pairs (median 71 kb) is substantially larger than between interacting E-P pairs (median 30 kb), supporting the possibility of indirect activation (Figure 4c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by distance distribution analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claims.claim: 59 of 366 verified E-P pairs show CTCF occupancy at enhancer side, and 13 of these lack E-P interaction in MChIP-C.
claims.source: Indeed, 59 of 366 verified E-P pairs show CTCF occupancy at enhancer side, and 13 of these lack E-P interaction in MChIP-C.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CTCF binding in CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs.

claims.claim: The fraction of verified E-P pairs in which spatial interaction is observed is likely underestimated.
claims.source: In summary, we conclude that the fraction of verified E-P pairs in which we observe a spatial interaction is likely underestimated, which further supports the notion that most enhancers physically interact with their targets and that many such interactions may have not been identified previously due to technical limitations of the employed methods.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the analysis of cases where interactions were missed and the reasons for missing them.

claims.claim: Most enhancers physically interact with their targets and many such interactions may have not been identified previously due to technical limitations of the employed methods.
claims.source: In summary, we conclude that the fraction of verified E-P pairs in which we observe a spatial interaction is likely underestimated, which further supports the notion that most enhancers physically interact with their targets and that many such interactions may have not been identified previously due to technical limitations of the employed methods.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the high rate of E-P interactions detected by MChIP-C compared to other methods and the analysis of missed interactions.

claims.claim: MChIP-C integrates proximity ligation of MNase-digested chromatin with chromatin immunoprecipitation and deep sequencing.
claims.source: In this study, we present a new high-resolution genome-wide C-method, MChIP-C, which integrates proximity ligation of MNase-digested chromatin with chromatin immunoprecipitation and deep sequencing.
claims.evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the Discussion and is supported by the Methods section.

claims.claim: MChIP-C allows precise mapping of localized chromatin interactions including E-P contacts which often evade capture by restriction endonuclease-based C-methods.
claims.source: Like other MNase-based C-methods, MChIP-C allows precise mapping of localized chromatin interactions including E-P contacts which often evade capture by restriction endonuclease-based C-methods (Goel and Hansen, 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the comparative analyses with restriction enzyme-based methods and a citation to a review.

claims.claim: MChIP-C uniquely combines the resolution and sensitivity of MCC with the genome-wide scale of Micro-C.
claims.source: Uniquely, MChIP-C combines the resolution and sensitivity of MCC with the genome-wide scale of Micro-C.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design and comparative analyses showing MChIP-C's advantages.

claims.claim: Tens of thousands of localized spatial interactions between promoters and distal genomic sites were mapped using H3K4me3-directed MChIP-C in K562 cells.
claims.source: Applying H3K4me3-directed MChIP-C to K562 cells, we explored the spatial connectivity of active promoters. Single-nucleosome resolution and high sensitivity allowed us to map tens of thousands of localized spatial interactions between promoters and distal genomic sites.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the interaction calling results presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Previously identified spatial contacts, such as contacts of globin gene promoters with their enhancers, are clearly visible in MChIP-C maps.
claims.source: The quality of the resulting genome-wide profiles is supported by the fact that previously identified spatial contacts, such as contacts of globin gene promoters with their enhancers, are clearly visible.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by visual inspection of MChIP-C profiles at known E-P interaction loci.

claims.claim: MChIP-C avoids the incorporation of biotin to enrich ligated fragments, thus yielding highly complex libraries.
claims.source: MChIP-C avoids the incorporation of biotin to enrich ligated fragments, thus yielding highly complex libraries.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design described in the Methods section.

claims.claim: Full realization of MChIP-C potential currently requires a significant sequencing depth due to the small fraction of informative reads.
claims.source: Consequently, full realization of MChIP-C potential currently requires a significant sequencing depth due to the small fraction of informative reads.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the observation that only ~4% of reads are informative (>5kb apart).

claims.claim: Further experimental optimizations of MChIP-C could significantly increase the method's yield.
claims.source: We anticipate that further experimental optimizations of MChIP-C could significantly increase the method's yield.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation about future improvements to the method.

claims.claim: Promoters appear to interact primarily with the surrounding CTCF sites.
claims.source: In agreement with previous observations, promoters appear to interact primarily with the surrounding CTCF sites.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the finding that 20.6% of PIRs colocalize with CTCF-bound sites and by citations to previous observations.

claims.claim: CTCF-motifs in promoter-interacting CTCF sites are typically oriented towards the interacting promoter.
claims.source: Interestingly, CTCF-motifs in these sites are typically oriented towards the interacting promoter (Valton et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the orientation bias analysis shown in Figure 3a and a citation to a related study.

claims.claim: The observed CTCF orientation bias can be explained by the putative ability of active promoters to block movement of the loop extrusion complex.
claims.source: This observation can be explained by the putative ability of active promoters to block movement of the loop extrusion complex which can lead to the establishment of promoter-CTCF loops with CTCF motifs preferentially oriented towards the promoters (Figure 3a, i; Banigan et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: The claim is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by a citation to a modeling study.

claims.claim: The observed CTCF orientation bias might be a consequence of architectural stripes, where a CTCF-bound site blocks loop extrusion in a directional manner.
claims.source: Alternatively, the observed bias might be a consequence of a more general phenomenon known as architectural stripes, where a CTCF-bound site blocks loop extrusion in a directional manner, causing nonspecific interactions with an extended nearby region (Vian et al., 2018; which may include the gene promoter; Figure 3a, ii).
claims.evidence: The claim is an alternative mechanistic hypothesis supported by a citation to a study on architectural stripes.

claims.claim: MChIP-C is sensitive enough to identify many relatively weak chromatin interactions that are independent of CTCF binding.
claims.source: Similarly to other MNase-based C-methods, MChIP-C is sensitive enough to identify many relatively weak chromatin interactions that are independent of CTCF binding.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the identification of 7214 regulatory interactions in cluster 3 DHSs that lack CTCF binding.

claims.claim: 7214 interactions linking active promoters with distal DHSs bound by a set of enhancer-specific factors were identified.
claims.source: We identified 7214 interactions linking active promoters with distal DHSs bound by a set of enhancer-specific factors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis and interaction calling results.

claims.claim: DHSs in regulatory interactions are highly enriched with functionally verified K562 regulatory sequences and contain chromatin marks typical for active enhancers.
claims.source: These DHSs are highly enriched with functionally verified K562 regulatory sequences and contain chromatin marks typical for active enhancers (Figure 3c; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis of CRISPRi-verified enhancers and ChromHMM state analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: The increased proximity between promoters and enhancer-like DHSs presumably represents regulatory E-P interactions.
claims.source: The increased proximity between promoters and these enhancer-like DHSs presumably represents regulatory E-P interactions.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the characteristics of cluster 3 DHSs and their interactions.

claims.claim: The E-P looping model assumes that direct physical contact between an enhancer and its target promoter is an essential prerequisite for the promoter activation.
claims.source: One of the long-standing hypotheses explaining enhancer action at a distance is the E-P looping model (Popay and Dixon, 2022; Ptashne, 1986) which assumes that direct physical contact between an enhancer and its target promoter is an essential prerequisite for the promoter activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citations to foundational papers on the E-P looping model.

claims.claim: Technical limitations of methods assessing spatial proximity and scarcity of functional data on mammalian enhancers prevented accurate systematic evaluation of the E-P looping model.
claims.source: Although it is known that at least some enhancers do establish physical contacts with their targets, technical limitations of methods assessing spatial proximity as well as scarcity of functional data on mammalian enhancers prevented accurate systematic evaluation of the E-P looping model.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the limitations of previous studies.

claims.claim: The highly dynamic nature of E-P interactions may preclude capturing them with existing proximity ligation techniques.
claims.source: To explain the elusiveness of E-P interactions, it has been suggested that their highly dynamic nature may preclude capturing with existing proximity ligation techniques (Schoenfelder and Fraser, 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review discussing the challenges of detecting E-P interactions.

claims.claim: It is likely that the majority of active enhancers directly interact with target promoters.
claims.source: Thus, it is likely that the majority of active enhancers directly interact with target promoters.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the finding that 60.7% (likely underestimated) of CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs show MChIP-C interactions.

claims.claim: MChIP-C found many apparently non-functional interactions of promoters with DHSs which did not show a significant effect on gene expression in CRISPRi screens.
claims.source: In addition to identifying interactions between promoters and their CRISPRi-validated enhancers, MChIP-C found many more apparently non-functional interactions of promoters with DHSs which did not show a significant effect on gene expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the finding that 6.5% of non-regulatory DHS-P pairs show MChIP-C interactions.

claims.claim: Non-functional interactions observed in MChIP-C could include structural loops as well as pre-established interactions of promoters with conditionally-activated regulatory elements.
claims.source: Such interactions are also often observed in alternative C-methods, and in some cases could represent CRISPRi false negative pairs. These interactions could also include structural loops as well as pre-established interactions of promoters with conditionally-activated regulatory elements (Jin et al., 2013; Comoglio et al., 2018), and warrant further investigation leveraging the increased sensitivity and resolution of MChIP-C.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation about the nature of non-functional interactions, supported by citations to relevant studies.

claims.claim: It is possible that DNA ends available for ligation can scan a certain territory within fixed nuclei, and thus MChIP-C detected interactions do not exactly represent direct physical contacts.
claims.source: Although it is generally assumed that in the C-methods ligation occurs only between fragments that are in close spatial proximity, the mobility of DNA ends within fixed nuclei has not been extensively studied. It is possible that DNA ends available for ligation can scan a certain territory and thus MChIP-C detected interactions do not exactly represent direct physical contacts.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation about the technical limitations and interpretation of C-methods.

claims.claim: The data demonstrates that, in most cases, enhancers establish some form of spatial interaction with their targets, resulting in increased ligation frequency.
claims.source: However, we argue that our data demonstrates that, in most cases, enhancers establish some form of spatial interaction with their targets, resulting in increased ligation frequency.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the high rate of E-P interactions detected by MChIP-C for CRISPRi-verified pairs.

claims.claim: Testing whether spatial interaction is necessary for gene activity would require understanding the physical nature of these interactions.
claims.source: Although we have shown that active mammalian enhancers in general interact with the target promoters, we cannot infer that this interaction is necessary for target activation. Testing whether it is possible to decouple spatial interactions from gene activity would require understanding the physical nature of these interactions.
claims.evidence: The claim is a statement about the limitations of the current study and future research directions.

claims.claim: Various protein factors and physical mechanisms including canonical protein-protein interactions, molecular crowding and liquid-liquid phase separation were implicated in E-P interactions.
claims.source: Various protein factors and a number of physical mechanisms including canonical protein-protein interactions, molecular crowding and liquid-liquid phase separation were implicated in this phenomenon (Kagey et al., 2010; Papantonis and Cook, 2013; Hnisz et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies proposing different mechanisms for E-P interactions.

claims.claim: Cohesin complex was suggested to be involved in E-P interactions, but recent studies exploring cellular responses to acute loss of cohesin found almost no overlap between regulatory E-P interactions and cohesin binding.
claims.source: One protein complex which was suggested to be involved is cohesin (Kagey et al., 2010; Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013). However, in line with studies exploring cellular responses to the acute loss of the cohesin complex (Thiecke et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2022), we observed almost no overlap between regulatory E-P interactions and cohesin binding.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the observation of cohesin absence in cluster 3 DHSs and citations to recent cohesin depletion studies.

claims.claim: Different groups proposed mediator complex, BRD4, YY1 and RNA polymerase II as candidates for mediating E-P interactions.
claims.source: Different groups proposed other candidates for the role: the mediator complex, BRD4, YY1 and RNA polymerase II (Kagey et al., 2010; Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013; Hnisz et al., 2017; Weintraub et al., 2017; Papantonis and Cook, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies proposing these factors as mediators of E-P interactions.

claims.claim: Recent studies did not identify drastic changes in E-P interaction frequency caused by the degradation or inhibition of mediator, BRD4, YY1, or RNA polymerase II.
claims.source: However, recent studies did not identify drastic changes in E-P interaction frequency caused by the degradation or the inhibition of any of these proteins (Ramasamy et al., 2022; Crump et al., 2021; Hsieh et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies testing the role of these factors in E-P interactions.

claims.claim: EP300 and SWI/SNF have rarely been considered as mediators of E-P interaction.
claims.source: Unlike cohesin, mediator, BRD4, YY1 and RNA polymerase II, EP300 and SWI/SNF have rarely been considered as mediators of E-P interaction.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on a review of the literature on E-P interaction mechanisms.

claims.claim: EP300 and SWI/SNF consistently outperformed other enhancer-associated factors in terms of predictive power for MChIP-C signal.
claims.source: However, in our analysis, they consistently outperformed other enhancer-associated factors in terms of predictive power.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the random forest modeling results shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claims.claim: The potential role of EP300 and SWI/SNF in E-P interaction warrants further experimental exploration.
claims.source: Although these results may be affected by differences in the quality of the ChIP-seq data, the potential role of EP300 and SWI/SNF in E-P interaction warrants further experimental exploration.
claims.evidence: The claim is a recommendation for future research based on the findings of the study.

claims.claim: EP300 and SWI/SNF are known as chromatin modifiers rather than structural proteins.
claims.source: Since both EP300 and SWI/SNF are known as chromatin modifiers rather than structural proteins (albeit some studies suggest such a role for EP300 Ma et al., 2021), it is possible that their participation in E-P interaction is indirect.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the functions of EP300 and SWI/SNF, with a citation noting an exception.

claims.claim: It is possible that EP300 and SWI/SNF participation in E-P interaction is indirect.
claims.source: Since both EP300 and SWI/SNF are known as chromatin modifiers rather than structural proteins (albeit some studies suggest such a role for EP300 Ma et al., 2021), it is possible that their participation in E-P interaction is indirect.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism by which EP300 and SWI/SNF might influence E-P interactions.

claims.claim: H3K27 residue is a well-documented EP300 nucleosomal target.
claims.source: Although H3K27 residue is a well-documented EP300 nucleosomal target (Tie et al., 2009), a recent study identified several other lysine residues localized in H2B N-terminus that are acetylated by EP300 (Weinert et al., 2018; Narita et al., 2022a; Narita et al., 2022b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on EP300 substrate specificity.

claims.claim: A recent study identified several lysine residues localized in H2B N-terminus that are acetylated by EP300.
claims.source: Although H3K27 residue is a well-documented EP300 nucleosomal target (Tie et al., 2009), a recent study identified several other lysine residues localized in H2B N-terminus that are acetylated by EP300 (Weinert et al., 2018; Narita et al., 2022a; Narita et al., 2022b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies on EP300 substrate specificity.

claims.source: These H2B N-terminus acetylation marks correlate with the enhancer activity more strongly than H3K27ac and therefore qualify for being involved in E-P interaction.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the cited studies showing stronger correlation of H2B acetylation with enhancer activity.

claims.claim: H2B N-terminus acetylation marks qualify for being involved in E-P interaction.
claims.source: These H2B N-terminus acetylation marks correlate with the enhancer activity more strongly than H3K27ac and therefore qualify for being involved in E-P interaction.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the correlation of H2B acetylation with enhancer activity.

claims.claim: 20.6% of PIRs colocalize with CTCF-bound sites.
claims.source: First, we observed that in MChIP-C 20.6% of PIRs colocalize with CTCF-bound sites (Figure 1c; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of PIRs with CTCF ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Both CTCF-bound and CTCF-less DHSs show increased interaction signal relative to background in MChIP-C.
claims.source: We thus separately examined DHSs with and without CTCF, and found that both types of DHSs show increased interaction signal relative to background.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of MChIP-C signal at DHSs shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: 50% downsampling of MChIP-C data maintains 76.3% of the detected interactions.
claims.source: We first observe that although the down-sampling suggests our MChIP-C data is not yet saturated by sequencing depth (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), 50% downsampling still maintains 76.3% of the detected interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by downsampling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

results.result: MChIP-C is a novel MNase-based proximity ligation method that combines chromatin immunoprecipitation with MNase digestion, avoiding biotin enrichment to yield highly complex libraries. The method was applied to K562 cells using H3K4me3 antibodies, generating ~3.5B read pairs with ~4% informative reads (>5kb apart), comparable to MCC but lower than restriction enzyme-based methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C21-C28, C90, and C95 collectively describe the MChIP-C method and its experimental implementation. The experimental design is clearly documented in the Methods section, sequencing statistics are provided, and the low fraction of informative reads is acknowledged and compared to other methods. The technical approach is well-supported by the data presented.

results.result: MChIP-C demonstrates superior resolution and sensitivity compared to restriction enzyme-based methods (PLAC-seq, Hi-C) and outperforms whole-genome Micro-C for promoter-centered interactions. MChIP-C shows 2.66-fold median enrichment at DHS centers versus PLAC-seq (1.25-fold) and Micro-C (1.51-fold), with 60.7% recall for CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs compared to 14.0% (PLAC-seq), 19.9% (Micro-C), and 2.2% (Hi-C).
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C41-C48, C77-C81, C91-C92 are strongly supported by systematic comparative analyses shown in Figures 2 and 4. Both visual comparisons and quantitative metrics (signal-to-noise ratios, recall/precision statistics) consistently demonstrate MChIP-C's advantages. The downsampling analysis (C79-C80) controls for sequencing depth differences, strengthening the conclusions.

results.result: MChIP-C identified 11,743 consensus H3K4me3 peaks that colocalize with active RNA Pol II TSSs, yielding single-nucleosome resolution interaction profiles for 10,955 active promoters. The method detected 112,087 promoter-promoter (P-P) and 128,986 promoter-nonpromoter (P-PIR) interactions, with 70-87% of interactions in each replicate reproducible across replicates.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C37 describe the data processing and interaction calling results. The high inter-replicate correlations (0.83-0.97 for merged profiles, 0.62-0.75 for viewpoint-specific profiles) and reproducibility statistics (70-87% of interactions present in multiple replicates) support the quality and reliability of the identified interactions. The numbers are clearly documented in the Results and supplementary materials.

results.result: MChIP-C profiles show clear, highly-localized interaction peaks at known regulatory elements, including detection of interactions between the MYC promoter and five of seven characterized K562-specific enhancers (e1-e7), and previously identified contacts such as globin gene promoter-enhancer interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 and C94 are supported by visual inspection of MChIP-C profiles at well-characterized loci (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a). The ability to detect known E-P interactions serves as positive validation of the method's sensitivity and accuracy. The specific example of MYC enhancers provides concrete evidence of the method's performance.

results.result: Promoters preferentially interact with CTCF-bound sites when CTCF motifs are oriented towards the promoter (79% towards vs 21% away), regardless of CTCF binding at the promoter side or position relative to transcription direction. Only ~2.7% of promoter-CTCF interactions with bilateral CTCF binding correspond to previously reported CTCF-CTCF loops, suggesting the orientation bias may involve loop extrusion mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54, C98-C99 are supported by systematic analysis of CTCF motif orientation in PIRs (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The orientation bias is quantified and shown to be consistent across different configurations. The comparison with Hi-C loops (C50) provides important context. The mechanistic interpretation (C54) is appropriately presented as a hypothesis based on the observed bias.

results.result: Most transcription-related factors and histone modifications are substantially enriched in MChIP-C PIRs (4-25X), with CTCF, RAD21, and SMC3 among the most highly enriched. Notable exceptions include H3K27me3 (not enriched) and 20.6% of PIRs colocalizing with CTCF-bound sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 and C128 are supported by systematic enrichment analysis of 271 ChIP-seq profiles (Figure 3b, Supplementary file 1). The enrichment calculations compare observed overlaps with expected values from random permutations, providing statistical rigor. The identification of exceptions (H3K27me3, ZNF146) demonstrates thorough analysis.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering of 19,129 PIR-overlapping DHSs identified four major clusters: clusters 1-2 (structural, CTCF/cohesin-bound, ~92kb median distance) and clusters 3-4 (regulatory, CTCF/cohesin-depleted, enriched for enhancer-specific factors). Cluster 3 DHSs show significant enrichment for CRISPRi-verified enhancers (171/297, p=1.64×10⁻⁵⁷) and 7,214 regulatory interactions with shorter median distance (~47kb).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64, C103-C105 describe a comprehensive clustering analysis supported by Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The statistical enrichment of CRISPRi-verified enhancers in cluster 3 (C62) provides strong validation. The observation of cohesin absence in regulatory interactions (C64) is supported by data and consistent with recent literature. The characterization of different interaction types is well-documented.

results.result: Random forest modeling identified EP300 and SWI/SNF complex subunits (DPF2, ARID1B, SMARCE1) as strong predictors of MChIP-C signal, increasing model R² from ~37% (distance + CTCF) to ~43% with addition of RAD21 and EP300. EP300 and SWI/SNF subunits are highly enriched in cluster 3 regulatory DHSs (92.2-97.8% binding) and outperform previously proposed mediators (mediator complex, BRD4, YY1, RNA Pol II).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C65-C73, C120-C121 are supported by systematic random forest modeling (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 2c). The greedy forward feature selection approach is methodologically sound, and the predictive power of EP300/SWI/SNF is clearly demonstrated. The high correlation between EP300 and SWI/SNF binding profiles (0.65-0.70) and their co-enrichment in regulatory interactions provide converging evidence. The comparison with other factors strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: 60.7% (222/366, 95% CI [55.7%-65.7%]) of CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs show underlying spatial interactions in MChIP-C, compared to only 6.5% of non-regulatory DHS-P pairs. This fraction is likely underestimated due to technical limitations, supporting the conclusion that most functionally verified enhancers physically interact with their cognate promoters, consistent with the E-P looping model.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C74-C76, C88-C89, C109, C113 represent the central biological conclusion of the study. The comparison with CRISPRi data (Figure 4a) provides strong functional validation. The statistical analysis includes confidence intervals and appropriate controls (non-regulatory pairs). The discussion of potential underestimation (C88) due to low coverage, imprecise enhancer mapping, and indirect effects (C82-C87) demonstrates critical evaluation of the results.

results.result: Analysis of CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs without detected MChIP-C interactions reveals several explanations: weak interactions missed by calling algorithms (especially in low-coverage viewpoints, with 68.1% detection in high-coverage viewpoints), imprecise enhancer positioning from CRISPRi screens, indirect regulatory effects (median distance 71kb for non-interacting vs 30kb for interacting pairs), and CTCF-mediated insulator effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87 provide critical analysis of false negatives, supported by visual inspection (Figure 4b) and distance analysis (Figure 4c). The reanalysis of high-coverage viewpoints (C83) showing 68.1% detection rate strengthens the argument for underestimation. The mechanistic explanations (indirect effects, CTCF insulators) are supported by specific examples and distance distributions. This thorough analysis of limitations enhances the credibility of the main conclusions.

results.result: MChIP-C currently requires significant sequencing depth due to the small fraction (~4%) of informative reads, though 50% downsampling maintains 76.3% of detected interactions. Further experimental optimizations could potentially increase the method's yield.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 and C130 acknowledge a key limitation of the method. The downsampling analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c-d) demonstrates that the data is not yet saturated, supporting C96. The statement about future optimizations (C97) is appropriately presented as speculation. This honest assessment of limitations is important for method evaluation.

results.result: Two mechanistic hypotheses are proposed to explain the observed CTCF orientation bias: (i) active promoters may block loop extrusion complex movement, establishing promoter-CTCF loops with preferentially oriented motifs, or (ii) the bias may result from architectural stripes where CTCF sites block loop extrusion directionally, causing nonspecific interactions with nearby regions including promoters.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 present mechanistic hypotheses supported by citations to modeling studies (Banigan et al., 2022; Vian et al., 2018). While the observed orientation bias is well-documented (C51-C53), these mechanistic explanations are speculative interpretations. The study does not provide direct experimental evidence to distinguish between these mechanisms or confirm either hypothesis. The claims are appropriately presented as possibilities rather than conclusions.

results.result: MChIP-C identified many apparently non-functional interactions (6.5% of non-regulatory DHS-P pairs), which could represent CRISPRi false negatives, structural loops, or pre-established interactions with conditionally-activated regulatory elements.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 acknowledge the presence of interactions not validated by CRISPRi screens. While the observation is data-supported (C75), the proposed explanations are speculative. The study does not provide additional experiments to characterize these interactions or test the proposed explanations. The claim appropriately notes that these interactions 'warrant further investigation,' acknowledging the uncertainty.

results.result: The study acknowledges that DNA ends may scan a territory within fixed nuclei, so detected interactions may not represent exact direct physical contacts. Additionally, while enhancers generally interact with target promoters, the study cannot determine whether spatial interaction is necessary for gene activation, which would require understanding the physical nature of these interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C112 and C114 represent important caveats about the interpretation of proximity ligation data. These are appropriately presented as limitations of the C-methods approach in general, not specific failures of the study. The acknowledgment that correlation between spatial proximity and function does not prove causation (C114) demonstrates scientific rigor. These are honest assessments of what can and cannot be concluded from the data.

results.result: EP300 and SWI/SNF are known as chromatin modifiers rather than structural proteins, suggesting their participation in E-P interactions may be indirect. Recent studies identified H2B N-terminus lysine residues acetylated by EP300 that correlate more strongly with enhancer activity than H3K27ac, potentially qualifying them for involvement in E-P interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C127 present mechanistic speculation about how EP300/SWI/SNF might mediate E-P interactions. While the predictive power of these factors is well-established (C66-C71), the mechanistic interpretation is speculative. The citations to studies on H2B acetylation (C125-C126) provide some support, but the study does not experimentally test whether these modifications are involved in E-P interactions. The claims are appropriately hedged with 'possible' and 'may,' but remain speculative.

results.result: The Introduction provides historical context on the E-P looping model, C-methods development, and previous attempts to identify factors mediating E-P interactions. It notes that direct evidence for E-P looping has been scarce, some enhancers lack detectable spatial proximity to targets, and recent studies found limited roles for previously proposed mediators (cohesin, mediator, BRD4, YY1, RNA Pol II).
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C20 and C106-C119 provide literature review and context. These are well-supported by appropriate citations to foundational and recent papers. The characterization of the field's state of knowledge appears accurate based on the cited literature. These claims establish the rationale for the study but do not represent novel findings from the current work.

results.result: MChIP-C is a novel MNase-based proximity ligation method that combines the genome-wide throughput of HiChIP with the exceptional resolution and sensitivity of MCC, allowing measurement of protein-mediated chromatin interactions at single-nucleosome resolution on a genome-wide scale.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm the technological advance. The editor states 'the evidence presented in this manuscript is convincing, and the technological advancements will be valuable.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the new method significantly increases the resolution of Micro-C' and 'the paper represented a significant technological advance.' Reviewer 3 states 'Methods appear to hold promise to improve both the sensitivity and resolution of protein-centered chromatin capture approaches.'

results.result: MChIP-C demonstrates greatly improved resolution and sensitivity compared to restriction endonuclease-based C-methods (PLAC-seq, Hi-C) and outperforms standard whole-genome Micro-C when applied to study H3K4me3 promoter-centered interactions in K562 cells, with superior recall (60.7% vs 14.0% PLAC-seq, 19.9% Micro-C, 2.2% Hi-C) for detecting CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 requests that the authors 'should show at least 2-3 cases' where MChIP-C detects E-P interactions not identified by other C-methods, indicating the comparative claims need more specific validation. Reviewer 1 also notes the comparison is 'not convincing since they only compared their data to one dataset. More datasets from other cell lines should be included.' While reviewers acknowledge the method's promise, they question the sufficiency of the comparative evidence.

results.result: EP300 histone acetyltransferase and the SWI/SNF remodeling complex are identified as potential candidates for establishing and/or maintaining enhancer-promoter interactions, outperforming other enhancer-associated factors (RNA polymerase II, mediator complex, YY1, BRD4) in predictive power for MChIP-C signal.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly requests 'More explanation is needed for this point since they're previously suggested to be associated with E-P interactions' regarding why EP300 and SWI/SNF are identified over other candidates. This indicates the reviewers find the evidence and reasoning insufficient to fully support the claim that EP300 and SWI/SNF are the key mediators, particularly given prior literature on other factors.

results.result: Most functionally verified enhancers (60.7% of CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs) physically interact with their cognate promoters as detected by MChIP-C, supporting the enhancer-promoter looping model, with this fraction likely underestimated due to technical factors.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'it's intriguing to see whether the MChIP-C could indeed detect the E-P interactions which were not identified by C-methods as they mentioned' and requests specific examples, indicating the main conclusion needs stronger validation. Reviewer 1 also questions 'The reasons to choose Chen's data and CRISPRi screens should be provided since there are so many out there,' suggesting concerns about the generalizability of the findings.

results.result: Four biological replicates of MChIP-C on K562 cells yielded ~3.5B read pairs with high reproducibility, identifying 112,087 P-P and 128,986 P-PIR interactions, though only ~4% of reads are informative, requiring significant sequencing depth.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'Downsampling analysis gives a better idea of the strengths of the approach' and acknowledges the technical sophistication. Reviewer 2 states 'the authors have addressed all my concerns and comments,' suggesting the experimental execution and data quality are accepted. The limitation of sequencing depth is acknowledged by reviewers as a technical consideration rather than a fundamental flaw.

results.result: Promoters preferentially interact with CTCF-bound sites when CTCF motifs are oriented towards the promoter (79% towards vs 21% away), suggesting possible involvement of loop extrusion mechanisms.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges these findings about CTCF orientation bias. The mechanistic interpretations are presented as possibilities consistent with loop extrusion models, and reviewers do not question this analysis or interpretation.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering of PIR-overlapping DHSs identified four major clusters: clusters 1-2 enriched in CTCF/cohesin (structural interactions), and cluster 3 enriched in CRISPRi-confirmed enhancers and transcription factors but lacking cohesin (7,214 regulatory interactions), suggesting cohesin may not be involved in maintaining regulatory interactions.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges the clustering analysis or the characterization of different interaction types. The findings about cohesin absence in regulatory interactions are consistent with recent literature cited by the authors, and reviewers do not dispute this interpretation.

results.result: Analysis of cases where CRISPRi-verified E-P pairs lack MChIP-C interactions reveals technical factors (low coverage, imprecise enhancer localization, indirect effects, CTCF interference) that likely lead to underestimation of the true E-P interaction rate.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this analysis of missed interactions. The discussion of technical limitations and factors affecting detection is presented as a reasonable interpretation of the data, and no reviewer disputes these explanations.

results.result: MChIP-C avoids biotin enrichment to yield highly complex libraries, but full realization of the method's potential requires significant sequencing depth due to the small fraction of informative reads (~4%), though further optimizations could increase yield.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 requests 'The limitations of the method should be discussed.' Reviewer 3 notes 'it remains technically sophisticated and for some labs may not be worth the additional effort for the increase in information,' acknowledging both the method's strengths and practical limitations. The authors' discussion of limitations appears to satisfy reviewer concerns.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on claims C82-C87 regarding false negatives and missed interactions. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support the analysis of technical limitations and factors affecting detection. OpenEval provides detailed validation of the mechanistic explanations, while peer reviewers accept these interpretations without challenge.

Significant disagreement on the central biological conclusion (C4, C74, C76, C88-C89, C109). OpenEval finds these claims SUPPORTED with strong functional validation from CRISPRi data, while peer reviewers rate them UNCERTAIN, requesting specific examples and questioning the generalizability of findings. Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly states the main conclusion needs stronger validation.

Disagreement on EP300/SWI/SNF as key mediators (C3, C66-C73, C120). OpenEval finds the random forest modeling and predictive power analysis SUPPORTED, while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 requesting more explanation for why these factors are identified over other candidates previously associated with E-P interactions.

Disagreement on comparative performance claims (C2, C41-C48, C77-C81). OpenEval finds systematic comparative analyses SUPPORTED with strong quantitative evidence, while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting comparisons are 'not convincing' due to limited datasets and requesting 2-3 specific cases where MChIP-C detects interactions missed by other methods.

Agreement on clustering analysis and interaction characterization (C58-C64, C103-C105). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support these findings. OpenEval highlights the statistical validation with CRISPRi data and cohesin observations, while peer reviewers do not challenge the clustering or characterization of different interaction types.

Agreement on CTCF orientation bias findings (C49-C54, C98-C99). Both rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the systematic quantification and appropriate presentation of mechanistic interpretation as hypothesis, while peer reviewers accept the findings without challenge, consistent with loop extrusion models.

Agreement on technological advance (C1, C21, C90). Both support the MChIP-C method development. OpenEval emphasizes clear documentation and technical implementation, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm the technological advance with editor and multiple reviewers noting it as 'convincing' and 'significant.' Peer result also includes C92 on comparative advantages.

Agreement on data processing and reproducibility (C29-C37). OpenEval finds high inter-replicate correlations and reproducibility statistics SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also support the technical execution (C25-C32, C34-C35, C96), with Reviewer 3 noting the downsampling analysis demonstrates technical sophistication, though they focus more on sequencing depth limitations.

Agreement on method limitations (C95-C97). Both support the acknowledgment of sequencing depth limitations and need for optimization. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on downsampling analysis showing data not yet saturated. Peer reviewers also support this, with reviewers acknowledging both technical sophistication and practical limitations.

Partial overlap on CTCF mechanistic hypotheses (C100-C101). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative interpretations without direct experimental evidence. Peer result R6 supports broader CTCF findings (C51-C54, C99) including mechanistic possibilities, with no reviewer challenges. Different scope but overlapping mechanistic claims.

Partial overlap on detection of known interactions (C38-C40, C94). OpenEval finds validation at well-characterized loci SUPPORTED. Peer result R2 addresses broader comparative claims including C38, C40 but rates UNCERTAIN due to insufficient comparative evidence across datasets. Different focus but overlapping validation claims.

Partial overlap on ChIP-seq enrichment analysis (C55-C57, C128). OpenEval supports the systematic enrichment analysis of 271 profiles. Peer result R7 supports clustering and interaction characterization (C55, C57 overlap) without challenge. Both agree on the quality of chromatin feature analysis.

OpenEval identifies claims C110-C111 about interactions not validated by CRISPRi as UNCERTAIN, noting speculative explanations that warrant further investigation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific claims about unvalidated interactions.

OpenEval supports claims C112, C114 as appropriate caveats about proximity-function correlation and limitations of C-methods approaches. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these interpretive limitations.

OpenEval rates claims C122-C127 about EP300/SWI/SNF mechanistic speculation as UNCERTAIN, noting appropriately hedged but experimentally untested hypotheses about H2B acetylation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific mechanistic speculations.

OpenEval supports claims C5-C20, C106-C119 as well-cited literature review and context establishing study rationale. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers typically do not evaluate background literature claims.
